title: Cron expressions explained: fields, time zones and next run times
description: Cron five-field order, how star, step, range and list stack, the second and year fields in 6/7-field forms, the day-weekday OR rule, checked with real runs.
content:
*/5 * * * * reads as every 5 minutes: the five fields are minute, hour, day, month and weekday in that order. The expression itself carries neither a time zone nor a command, so the actual run time is decided by the scheduler's time zone.

1. Five fields, one each, in a fixed order

The standard five-field form has a fixed order: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. The allowed values in crontab(5) are: minute 0-59, hour 0-23, day 1-31, month 1-12, weekday 0-7, where both 0 and 7 mean Sunday. The day starts at 1, so writing 0 there is out of range.

FieldMeaningAllowed valuesOne reading measured in this tool
Field 1Minute0-59*/5 is every 5 minutes
Field 2Hour0-239 is the 9 o'clock hour
Field 3Day of month1-311 is the 1st of each month
Field 4Month1-12* is every month
Field 5Weekday0-71-5 is Monday to Friday

The habit when reading an expression is to confirm "which day" from the right first, then "which moment" moving left, because month and weekday decide the trigger day while minute and hour only decide the time of day on that date.

2. Star, slash, hyphen and comma can stack

The star means every value in that field; the slash means a step starting from the field's minimum; the hyphen is an inclusive range; the comma is a union. The four forms combine, so 0-30/10 means the four minute values 0, 10, 20 and 30.

The most common slip is writing "every 5 minutes" as 5 * * * *. In */5 the minute field is a step; the 5 in the minute field is a constant: measured over the first three runs, the former gives 04:05, 04:10 and 04:15, the latter gives 04:05, 05:05 and 06:05. The first run happens to match and the second one separates them, which is why this mistake is easy to overlook.

A step only acts inside its own field. The NOTES in crontab(5) make the point: */35 in the minute field is not once every 35 minutes, but minute 0 and minute 35 of every hour.

3. 5, 6 and 7 fields are three different layouts

The tool page hint states that it supports 5 fields (minute hour day month weekday), 6 fields (second minute hour day month weekday) and 7 fields (second minute hour day month weekday year). The 6-field form adds an extra seconds field at the front, and the 7-field form adds a year field at the end. That seconds field defaults to 0, so the 6-field 0 0 9 * * 1-5 and the 5-field 0 9 * * 1-5 produce the same list of results; but read the first two fields of the 6-field form as minute and hour and the whole line shifts by one column. Measured 30 * * * * *, the first run is 04:00:30, so field 2 really is 30.

The quickest way to decide the field count is to split on spaces and count: the number of non-empty pieces is the number of fields. The tool hard-validates that count, and any number other than 5, 6 or 7 is not guessed into another format.

The year field can pin a single year: 0 0 0 1 1 * 2028 yields one result, 2028-01-01, and no next run after it. Too few or too many fields are not guessed into another format either: * * * * reports a field-count error directly.

4. Months and weekdays accept names, but numbering depends on the implementation

Months and weekdays accept the first three letters of the English name, case-insensitively, and also work as ranges and lists: MON-FRI, JAN and mon,wed,fri all parse. Sunday is both 0 and 7, and a form like 0,7 is merged; measured, it gives four consecutive Sundays rather than two runs per week.

The numbering rule has one real cross-system difference: standard Vixie cron and this tool both use 0 or 7 for Sunday and 1 for Monday; the Quartz style uses 1 for Sunday and 7 for Saturday. The same digit 1 points at different days on the two sides. This tool's parser library offers a Quartz-numbering switch, but the tool page does not expose it, so the meaning on the page stays the standard numbering.

5. Day and weekday both restricted: the crontab(5) OR

crontab(5) says it plainly: if both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted (neither contains a star), the command runs when either one matches the current time. Its example is 30 4 1,15 * 5, meaning the 1st and 15th of each month plus every Friday.

This tool measures the same result: the next four runs of 0 9 1 * MON fall on 11-23, 11-30, 12-01 and 12-07; the first two are Mondays and the third is the 1st, so Monday and the 1st are a union. To require both at once, this tool accepts a plus sign before the weekday field: the next three runs of 0 9 1 * +MON are 2027-02-01, 2027-03-01 and 2027-11-01, the days when the 1st happens to be a Monday. That plus is an extension of the pattern spec used by this tool. The Quartz side does not allow day and weekday to be restricted at once: restricting both is rejected by the parser, so one of them has to become ? when migrating, which is why this has to be confirmed before switching systems.

6. ?, L, W and # are not universal syntax

These enhanced characters work in some implementations. Measured in this tool: 0 0 L * * gives 11-30, 12-31 and 01-31, the last day of each month; 0 12 * * 5#2 gives 12-11 and 01-08, the second Friday of each month; 0 12 * * FRI#L gives 11-27 and 12-25, the last Friday of each month; 0 0 1W * * gives 2027-05-03 when 1 May 2027 is a Saturday; 0 9 ? * ? matches 0 9 * * * exactly, because the question mark equals the star.

But the field table in crontab(5) lists only four characters: star, comma, hyphen and slash, with no L, W, # or ?. These are extensions from Quartz and from parser libraries, and Linux crontab does not accept them. To reuse an expression across systems, delete the enhanced characters or build the same dates out of several plain expressions.

7. A 31st does not slide to 28 February

With 31 in the day field, months without a 31st simply have no run that day; they do not fall back to month end. Measured, the next five runs of 0 0 31 * * are 12-31, 01-31, 03-31, 05-31 and 07-31: months 2, 4, 6, 9 and 11 (February, April, June, September and November) never trigger. Only 7 months of the year run.

"Last day of the month" needs L or several expressions. 0 0 30 2 * is the other extreme: perfectly valid syntax, but February has no 30th, so it never triggers. Measured, it returns no execution time at all; the results area stays empty and the status reads "Valid expression, generated 0 execution times". A zero result is not the same as a mistake, so troubleshoot them separately. A leap day needs 0 0 29 2 *, which measured gives 2028-02-29, 2032-02-29 and 2036-02-29.

8. Why there is a parenthesis after each next run time

The tool page has no time zone selector and no note about time zones: it formats every result in Asia/Shanghai and appends a UTC ISO time in parentheses. The Z at the end of the ISO string means an offset of 0, the form RFC 3339 defines, so the part in parentheses is the only absolute value that does not shift with the display time zone.

The expression itself is interpreted in the runtime's local time zone: the page builds its parser without a time zone argument. Measured with the same 0 9 * * *, a UTC runtime lands on 09:00Z, an America/New_York runtime on 14:00Z and an Asia/Shanghai runtime on 01:00Z (already the next day); on screen the three read as the Shanghai clock showing 17:00, 22:00 and 09:00 the next day. In other words, "9 o'clock" is the 9 o'clock you mean only when the browser's or server's time zone happens to equal the one in your head.

The Copy button on the right of the results area copies the whole block, including the ISO time in parentheses; when checking, do not take the leading Shanghai clock time for local time.

To compare a city's current offset, add that time zone in the World Clock and read them side by side; to convert the ISO string in parentheses to and from a second-level timestamp, the Timestamp Converter is more direct.

9. Across DST: the missing hour and the repeated hour

crontab(5) is blunt about daylight saving: a time that does not exist at the transition never matches, so jobs inside it do not run; when the same clock time occurs twice, a matching job runs twice.

Measured, this tool handles it differently. For America/New_York, 0 2 * * * on 2027-03-14: local 02:00 does not exist, and the result lands on 07:00Z, which is 03:00 on the New York clock, so the job did not vanish but hit the moment of the jump. */30 * * * * on the same day gives 01:00, 01:30, 03:00 and 03:30 on the local clock; the 02:00 and 02:30 slots simply do not exist. On the fall-back day 2026-11-01, 0 1 * * * gives only 05:00Z, the first 01:00, and the repeated 01:00 does not run again.

So "once a day" does not always land on the hour you wrote on a transition day: on the gap day the slot disappears, and on the fall-back day it may run only the first time instead of twice. Keep important jobs out of the local 00:00 to 03:00 window, or record the actual execution time inside the job.

10. Macros like @daily save typing, not the time zone

A macro is a whole-line substitution: @daily and @midnight equal 0 0 * * *, @hourly equals 0 * * * *, @weekly equals 0 0 * * 0, @monthly equals 0 0 1 * *, and @yearly and @annually equal 0 0 1 1 *. Measured one by one, the two strings in each pair give identical results.

@reboot is the exception: this tool reports "@reboot is not supported in this environment" exactly, because a browser cannot detect a system reboot. A macro brings no time zone information either; what it expands into is still those five fields interpreted in the local time zone.

11. Which mistake each error message points at

The tool page shows an error as "Invalid expression:" followed by the parser library's original text. That text is English, but the keywords locate the field.

InputKeyword in the status barWhat is wrong
* * * *exactly five, six, or seven space separated partsWrong number of fields
60 * * * *Invalid value for minute: 60Minute out of range
0 0 0 0 0Invalid value for day: -1Day written as 0
*/0 * * * *illegal stepping: 0Step of 0
5/10 * * * *stepping with numeric prefixThe step prefix can only be a star or a range

Empty input gets its own message, "Please enter a Cron expression", and never reaches the parser. When a valid expression runs, the status bar reads "Valid expression, generated N execution times", where N is the selected preview count, one of 5, 10 or 20.

12. Checklist before going live

  1. Count the fields: 5, 6 or 7, and whether the seconds and year fields are present.
  2. Confirm whether day and weekday are an OR or an AND, and which numbering the target system uses.
  3. Find the enhanced characters (L, W, #, ?) and confirm the target scheduler supports them.
  4. Write the expression's time zone into the config or the docs; do not rely on the runtime default.
  5. Convert the UTC time in parentheses to the target time zone once, and check the transition days and month ends.
  6. Add a lock or an idempotent design for short-interval jobs, so a run cannot re-enter before the previous one has finished.

13. Scope and limits

Most of the semantic values here come from measurements of croner 10.0.1, the parser library behind the tool page; the page rendering and browser behaviour come from measurements in Chromium. A different version or scheduler may behave differently. The Cron Expression Tool only previews: it runs no command and validates no command, user or permission. The results area's time zone is hard-coded to Asia/Shanghai and reads no environment variable such as CRON_TZ. The DST section covers only America/New_York and the dates listed here; southern-hemisphere and half-hour-offset zones were not tested. Quartz's full syntax, systemd timers and the time zone fields in container orchestration are out of scope.

faqs.q: Why can't "every 5 minutes" be written as 5 * * * *?
faqs.a: In 5 * * * * the minute field is the constant 5, so it runs at minute 5 of every hour; every 5 minutes needs */5 * * * *, so the minute field takes a step. Both first run at 04:05; the second runs are 04:10 and 05:05.

faqs.q: With day 1 and weekday MON, is it an AND or an OR?
faqs.a: Standard Vixie cron and this tool default to OR: once on the 1st of each month, and again every Monday. To switch to AND, this tool takes a plus sign before the weekday field, written +MON; Quartz does not allow day and weekday to be restricted at once, so one of the two has to become ?, and restricting both is rejected by the parser. The AND form is a syntax this tool extends with the + modifier, so confirm it before changing systems.

faqs.q: Why do the next run times the tool shows differ from my expectation by several hours?
faqs.a: The time on that part of the page is a hard-coded Asia/Shanghai rendering, while the expression is interpreted in the browser's or runtime's local time zone. Trust the UTC time in parentheses (the trailing Z) and convert it to the target time zone.
